entities.name: Venus de Milo
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Venus de Milo, a stunning ancient Greek marble statue, embodies the peak of Hellenistic artistry and is believed to have been sculpted around 140 BCE, during a period marked by the cultural synthesis of Greek and Eastern influences. Discovered on the island of Melos in the Aegean Sea in 1820, this work is attributed to the famed sculptor Alexandros of Antioch, whose techniques exemplify the era's mastery of form and beauty. The statue represents the ideal of feminine beauty and is emblematic of the broader cultural currents of the time, which combined classical Greek aesthetics with new stylistic elements from the East, illustrating the interconnectedness of civilizations in antiquity.

Crafted during the late Hellenistic period, the Venus de Milo showcases the advanced sculptural techniques of its time, including a contrapposto stance and intricate drapery that enhances the figure's grace. Its discovery by a French naval officer, Olivier Voutier, and subsequent presentation to King Louis XVIII catalyzed a renewed interest in classical antiquity, influencing neoclassicism in art and architecture across Europe. The statue's missing arms have sparked extensive debate and restoration efforts, symbolizing the ongoing struggle to preserve and understand ancient artifacts amid the ravages of time and conflict.

The legacy of Venus de Milo extends beyond its physical presence; it has become a cultural icon representing not only beauty but also the complexities of identity and representation in art. Over the years, it has inspired countless works across various media, from literature to modern visual arts, and has been a focal point in discussions surrounding the role of women in art and society. Its status as a major tourist attraction in the Louvre underscores its significance in contemporary culture, drawing millions of visitors annually who seek to connect with a piece of history that continues to resonate today.
